summary: Defines Management Information Base objects for monitoring and controlling iFCP gateway instances and their sessions. It obsoletes RFC 4369 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A dashboard list of numbers and switches for watching and controlling a gateway that carries storage traffic over IP.

questions: how to monitor an ifcp gateway with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP management objects for watching and controlling iFCP gateways and the storage sessions that run through them.

tldr.problem: iFCP gateways carry Fibre Channel storage traffic over IP, and operators need a standard way to monitor and configure those gateways and their sessions with network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the IFCP-MGMT-MIB module, a set of SNMP objects arranged in tables for local gateway instances, iFCP sessions, and per-session statistics (with both 64-bit and 32-bit counters).
tldr.outcome: It replaces the first iFCP MIB, RFC 4369, mainly because iFCP address translation mode was deprecated, so the old compliance statement and session group are now marked deprecated.

today: RFC 6173 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4369, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the current definition of the iFCP MIB module.

sections.title: What the iFCP MIB Is For
sections.content:
iFCP (defined in RFC 4172) provides Fibre Channel fabric functionality on an IP network, where TCP/IP switching and routing elements replace Fibre Channel components. iFCP runs between iFCP gateways, which can be used by Fibre Channel to IP storage gateways for Fibre Channel Protocol (FCP) storage interconnects.

This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module so that a network management protocol such as SNMP can monitor and manage local iFCP gateway instances, including the configuration of iFCP sessions between gateways. Objects in the MIB are written with SMIv2, and the key words MUST, SHOULD and so on follow RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: Some gateways pass storage data across the internet. This RFC is the list of gauges and switches a manager can use to look after those gateways.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organised
sections.content:
The module is divided into three parts: local iFCP gateway instance management, iFCP session management, and iFCP session statistics. One management entity can monitor several local gateway instances. Each local gateway is conceptually an independent gateway with both Fibre Channel and IP interfaces.

The MIB only covers what is specific to iFCP. For other gateway parameters, the RFC points to standard MIBs such as the Fibre Management MIB (RFC 4044) or the Interfaces Group MIB (RFC 2863), and the local gateway section has optional links to them. The module imports types from several of these standard MIBs.

The module itself is registered at { transmission 230 } under the name ifcpMgmtMIB, the one IANA-assigned object identifier the document records.
sections.eli5: The control panel has three drawers: one for each gateway, one for each connection, and one for the counting numbers. Anything not about iFCP is kept in other panels.

sections.title: The Gateway Instance Table
sections.content:
The ifcpLclGtwyInstTable has one row per local iFCP gateway instance being managed, indexed by ifcpLclGtwyInstIndex. Its objects give the minimum and maximum iFCP protocol version the gateway supports, an optional pointer to the gateway's entry in the Entity MIB, a text description of up to 64 characters, and the current number of sessions in the open or open-pending state.

Several objects are read-write and set gateway-wide defaults: whether FC Broadcast is supported (default false), the default IP_TOV (the maximum time an encapsulated Fibre Channel frame may take to cross the IP network) and the default Liveness Test Interval (LTI). The IP_TOV range is 0 to 3600 seconds with a default of 6, and 0 means frame lifetime limits are not enforced. The LTI range is 0 to 65535 seconds with a default of 10, and 0 means no liveness test is used.

The RFC warns that changing the address translation mode or FC Broadcast support may disrupt existing sessions.
sections.eli5: Each gateway gets one line on a sheet. The line says what versions it speaks, how long a message may take to cross, and how often it checks that the other end is still there.

sections.title: iFCP Sessions
sections.content:
An iFCP session is a pair of N_PORTs (the endpoints) joined by a single TCP/IP connection. The ifcpSessionAttributesTable has a row for every session currently using a local gateway instance, indexed by the gateway instance and a session index. Gateways create and remove the sessions, and the table reflects that.

Each row records the local and remote portal addresses and TCP ports, the world wide unique names and Fibre Channel identifiers of the two N_PORTs, the IP_TOV and LTI values in use, and whether the session is bound to specific N_PORTs. Sessions are unbound by default. The remote TCP port normally holds the iFCP canonical port, 3420.

A session row should correspond to an entry in the TCP-MIB connection table, and both are deleted when the TCP connection ends. Per-session IP_TOV starts from the gateway default and can be changed for that session.
sections.eli5: Each live connection gets its own line: who is on each end, where they are, and the rules for that connection. When the connection ends, the line is erased.

sections.title: Session Statistics
sections.content:
Two tables extend the session table with counters. ifcpSessionStatsTable uses 64-bit counters for the session state, duration, octets and frames sent and received, stale frames discarded, header CRC errors, Fibre Channel payload CRC errors, and other errors. A discontinuity time object says when any of these counters last had a break.

ifcpSessionLcStatsTable offers the same counts as 32-bit counters for systems without 64-bit support. The RFC notes that at 1 Gbps a 32-bit counter can wrap as often as every 34 seconds, so the 64-bit table is recommended where possible. It also notes that a single header CRC error is usually enough to end a session.
sections.eli5: Two scoreboards count what each connection has sent, received and got wrong. One scoreboard has room for huge numbers, and the other is smaller and fills up quickly.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 4369
sections.content:
The only stated reason for the new version is that iFCP address translation mode is deprecated, as explained in RFC 6172 ("Deprecation of iFCP Address Translation Mode"). This document therefore obsoletes the earlier iFCP MIB, RFC 4369.

The module's revision history says the same thing. The conformance section now has two compliance statements. The original one is marked deprecated, and it required both addressTransparent(1) and addressTranslation(2). The new one, ifcpGatewayComplianceNoTranslation, is current and requires support only for addressTransparent(1). Likewise the original session group is deprecated, and a new group without the remote N_PORT alias object replaces it.
sections.eli5: One of the old ways of working was retired, so the checklist was rewritten without it. The old checklist stays in the book but is marked as out of date.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Read-write objects can be sensitive. Changing ifcpLclGtwyInstAddrTransMode, ifcpLclGtwyInstFcBrdcstSupport, either default timer, or ifcpSessionIpTOV may disrupt storage traffic. Changing ifcpLclGtwyInstDescr may cause a user to lose track of a gateway.

Readable objects can also be sensitive: the gateway instance table and the session attributes table can show who is communicating and exchanging storage data. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and the RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic mechanisms, and says deploying older versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must also make sure only legitimate principals can read or change the objects.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can turn these dials could upset the storage traffic, and anyone who can read them can see who is talking to whom. So only trusted people should get the keys, and the connection to the panel should be locked.
